name: Council on Strategic Risks (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: almost all the value is the biological and nuclear work, against catastrophes that kill people everywhere, so the result is spread by world population; the climate-security work (a few percent of the value) is mostly for the US and its allies.
summary: The Council on Strategic Risks (Washington DC) works against biological weapons and pandemics, nuclear risks and the security risks of climate change: its Nolan Center on Strategic Weapons (policy, dialogues with allied governments and four fellowships), its Center for Climate and Security and a small Converging Risks Lab; this model covers all its programmes in 2025 ($5.2M spent). At the defaults it averts about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, from {{low}} to {{high}} on its plausible range: after each branch's adjustments, about 68% of that is the fellowships (8% of the cost), counted through the work their alumni add, about 24% the nuclear work (about a quarter of the cost) and 8% the biological work (about a third), each dollar of those two valued as a typical project's cut in the forecast risks of nuclear war and pandemics (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts), with deaths valued like every death and the future lost counted only where you count lives that never start (0% by default); the climate-security work (over a third of the cost), valued as better use of the public money it bears on, almost nothing. The biggest uncertainty is how much a dollar of such work cuts the risk (Rethink calls its figures placeholders; the range runs ten times either way), and CSR doesn't say how the Nolan Center's spending splits between biological and nuclear work. Every branch is discounted for missing data: no outcome of the work is measured.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

story.sentence: $1,000 pays for work against pandemics, nuclear war and other catastrophes. Every **{1000 / (1000 * donor_cost_share * marginal_vs_past_average * deaths_averted / cost_total * total_adj)|$}** averts **a death** on average.

rows.label: Field-building: the fellowships' cost in 2025
rows.explainer: What the Nolan Center's four fellowships cost in the year (stipends, staff time, the travel and convenings they need): the Fellowship for Ending Bioweapons (part-time, ten months, with a stipend), the Nuclear Risk Reduction Fellowship, the Mid-Career Biodefense Bootcamp (a virtual course and an in-person workshop, travel paid) and the International Mid-Career Biosecurity Fellowship (a convening in Germany in June 2025). CSR doesn't split them out; travel and conferences together were $490,592 in 2025 (Part IX lines 17 and 19: 293,131 and 197,461), much of it for dialogues rather than fellows. $350,000, about 13% of the Nolan Center, $200,000 to $600,000, our judgment. Taken out of the Nolan Center's line before its bio and nuclear split, so nothing counts twice.

rows.label: Nolan Center: share of its other work on biological threats
rows.explainer: CSR doesn't split the Nolan Center's spending by area. The anchor is Coefficient Giving's November 2024 grant of $6,530,000 over three years, "to support its work on biosecurity fellowships and policy, as well as general operations" (https://www.longtermwiki.com/sourcing/grant/2Xx6G3L2L9): about $2.18M a year, less the biosecurity fellowships (about $280,000: fb_cost × fb_bio_share) and a general-operations part (about a quarter, $500,000, much of it management outside the programmes), leaves about $1.4M of biological policy work against the Center's $2.42M of other work (its line less the fellowships), 58%; other funders of its biological work (none named) push it up. The Center's page (https://councilonstrategicrisks.org/nolan) also gives biological threats the most projects (the Biodefense Budget Breakdown, the Global Biosecurity Accelerator, the Seoul and Berlin biosecurity dialogues) beside the nuclear ones (the Nuclear Weapons Systems Project, work on Iran and Kazakhstan, arms control). 60%, from 45% (the grant's general-operations part larger) to 80% (other bio funders and none of the grant on operations), our judgment; the rest is nuclear and arms control (chemical weapons have no programme of their own).

rows.label: Converging Risks Lab: share on nuclear risk
rows.explainer: The lab "currently includes the climate-nuclear-security project" (Form 990 Part III line 4c), on how climate change and an expansion of nuclear power bear on nuclear security and proliferation; its other work is foresight and ecological security (wildlife trafficking, biodiversity loss and security). Half, 25% to 75%, our judgment; the nuclear half is valued as nuclear field work, the rest in the gov branch.

rows.explainer: The Nolan Center's biological-threat work (its line less the fellowships, × csw_bio_share) over all programme spending: about {{row:bio_cost_share}}. Overhead is spread alike (cost_total).

rows.explainer: Everything else, about {{row:gov_cost_share}}: the Center for Climate and Security and the Converging Risks Lab's other half (foresight, ecological security), (ccs_line + crl_line × (1 − crl_nuclear_share)) over all programme spending. Their aim is that militaries, security agencies and governments plan and spend for climate risks as their scale warrants, so one chain values them as better use of public money.

rows.label: Climate security: public money a year in the programmes the work touches, per dollar spent
rows.explainer: The yearly public budgets whose use a dollar of the work bears on in 2025: before that year the US Defense Department's request for fiscal 2024 "proposes $5.1 billion in funding for 'enhancing combat capability and mitigating climate risk'", $3.7 billion of it for installation resilience (Congressional Research Service, IF12161, updated 6 April 2023, https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/IF12161.html); in 2025 the administration ended most of the department's climate programmes, so the US part is taken at half that at most, beside allied militaries' and NATO's climate-security work through the International Military Council on Climate and Security. Against about $1.9M a year of the work with overhead, $2-3 billion would be about 1,100 to 1,600 dollars per dollar; others work on it too, so 500, from 50 to 3,000 (the fiscal 2024 budget, all of it), our judgment.

rows.label: Share of public investment's value lost to inefficiency, advanced economies
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how much better public spending in rich countries could do (the IMF's efficiency gap for public investment, facts/democracy.json): the room the work can close. It is measured on investment and applied here to all the public spending the work touches, programmes and regulation too, for want of a figure for those; gov_gap_closed's wide range covers the difference.

rows.label: Climate security: share of that gap the work closes in the programmes it touches, a year
rows.explainer: Analysis, briefings and dialogues among many voices shape how militaries plan for climate risk only a little: 0.3% (0.03% to 2%), our judgment, with no reference class.

rows.label: Climate security: years from the spending until programmes change
rows.explainer: A recommendation taken up in a plan or budget takes about a year, our judgment, 0 to 3, as the catastrophic-risk branches; discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Climate security: discounted years a change counts
rows.explainer: A change in how a programme works counts the site's years for a won reform ($win_years_counted), after its wait, at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of US public good, in units of value
rows.explainer: A dollar more of what public money buys, valued like a dollar of consumption to the average American: one over the household survey's consumption per person (the Consumer Expenditure Survey, 2024, in 2025 dollars: the one scale for US public money, docs/normalization.md 2.14) in ln(consumption), × the shared value of doubling consumption. Allied militaries' spending serves countries about as rich. No marginal cost of public funds: better use of the same money costs the payers nothing more.

rows.label: Climate security: better public spending, in units of value (before adjustments)
rows.formula: cost_total * gov_cost_share * gov_public_dollars_per_dollar * gov_efficiency_gap * gov_gap_closed * gov_discounted_years * gov_value_per_public_dollar
rows.explainer: The branch's cost × public money touched per dollar × the share of its value lost to inefficiency × the share of that the work closes × the discounted years × the value of a dollar of US public good. Enters the result through the bridge from units of value (uov_bridged).

rows.label: Check: the cost shares add up to all the modelled spending
rows.formula: ai_cost_share + bio_cost_share + nuclear_cost_share + pol_cost_share + fb_cost_share + gov_cost_share
rows.explainer: Must be 1: the five branches' shares and the gov branch's add up to all programme spending.

rows.label: Deaths averted, every branch (expected, before adjustments)
Deaths averted that are in a COVID-scale pandemic (a part of deaths_averted)
rows.formula: bio_deaths_averted * bio_covid_scale_share + pol_deaths_averted * bio_covid_scale_share + fb_deaths_averted * fb_covid_scale_share
rows.explainer: A natural or zoonotic pandemic on COVID's scale kills mostly older people, so its deaths are valued at COVID-19's age mix; every other size at the world's. The policy branch (pointed at pandemics) adds its deaths × bio_covid_scale_share and the field-building branch its pandemic part (fb_covid_scale_share).

rows.label: Value of a death averted in a COVID-scale pandemic (units of value)
rows.explainer: As value_per_death, with the shared COVID-scale age mix (@death_ages.covid_scale_*): the one value of a death by age. Fixed.

rows.label: Future healthy years kept, every branch (expected, before adjustments)
Suffering of the farmed animals the people of that future would eat, in healthy years
rows.formula: -((cost_total * ai_cost_share / 1e6 * ai_future_per_million * ai_discounted_years) + (cost_total * bio_cost_share / 1e6 * bio_future_per_million * bio_discounted_years) + (cost_total * nuclear_cost_share / 1e6 * nuclear_future_per_million * nuclear_discounted_years) + (pol_wins * pol_p_success * pol_relative_cut * pol_future_per_year * pol_discounted_years) + (fb_work_dollars / 1e6 * fb_credit_share * fb_future_per_million * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, years_of_impact))) * $lives_added * $animal_dalys_per_person_year_world
rows.explainer: A future kept is also every animal raised to feed it: each future person-year at the suffering of the animals an average person eats in a year today (docs/normalization.md 2.25). Suffering always counts, whatever lives that never start count; the farmed animals' own good days count where you set them to. Held at today's diet: no forecast of what people will eat is used.

rows.label: Healthy years per unit of value of the deaths averted (for the weights below)
rows.explainer: The bridge's healthy years per unit of value, times the losses beyond deaths that only the deaths carry: turns each branch's deaths into healthy years for the weights. Written over uov_bridged because the gov branch's units of value go through the same bridge.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the AI work (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The branch's deaths averted in healthy years, plus its future healthy years kept: the weight its adjustments carry. Fixed.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the pandemic work (before adjustments)
rows.formula: bio_deaths_averted * ((1 - bio_covid_scale_share) * value_per_death + bio_covid_scale_share * covid_value_per_death) * dalys_per_death_value + bio_future_dalys
rows.explainer: The branch's deaths averted in healthy years (the COVID-scale part at COVID-19's age mix), plus its future healthy years kept: the weight its adjustments carry. Fixed.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the nuclear work (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The branch's deaths averted in healthy years, plus its future healthy years kept: the weight its adjustments carry. Fixed.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the policy win (before adjustments)
rows.formula: pol_deaths_averted * ((1 - bio_covid_scale_share) * value_per_death + bio_covid_scale_share * covid_value_per_death) * dalys_per_death_value + pol_future_dalys
rows.explainer: The policy branch's deaths averted in healthy years (pointed at pandemics, its COVID-scale part at COVID-19's age mix), plus its future healthy years kept; 0 here (pol_wins 0).

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the people trained (before adjustments)
rows.formula: fb_deaths_averted * ((1 - fb_covid_scale_share) * value_per_death + fb_covid_scale_share * covid_value_per_death) * dalys_per_death_value + fb_future_dalys
rows.explainer: The branch's deaths averted in healthy years (its COVID-scale part at COVID-19's age mix), plus its future healthy years kept: its share of the value, used to weight the adjustments.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the climate-security work (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The branch's units of value in healthy years: the weight its adjustments carry.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from every branch (before adjustments)
rows.formula: w_ai + w_bio + w_nuclear + w_pol + w_fb + w_gov

rows.label: AI field work: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: Not used: the AI branch has no spending (weight 0). The template's figure kept.

rows.label: Pandemic field work: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: How far Rethink Priorities' typical small pandemic project applies to the Nolan Center's biological-threat work: policy proposals on ending biological weapons and US biodefense (the Biodefense Budget Breakdown of federal spending), the Global Biosecurity Accelerator's dialogues with allied governments (Berlin, June 2025) and its Global Biosecurity Tracker (December 2025), led by former senior officials (Andrew Weber, once the Pentagon's Assistant Secretary for Nuclear, Chemical and Biological Defense Programs). Access to governments, but no uptake measured: 0.8 (0.3 to 1.2), our judgment.

rows.label: Nuclear field work (Nolan Center): how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: How far Rethink Priorities' typical small nuclear project applies to the Nolan Center's nuclear and arms-control work: reports (The Consequences of Tactical Nuclear Weapons Use, October 2025), the Nuclear Weapons Systems Project's record of every nuclear weapon the five recognised nuclear powers deployed, arguments on arms control and new systems; no uptake measured for 2025. 0.7 (0.3 to 1.2), the template's figure for typical policy work.

rows.label: Nuclear field work (Converging Risks Lab): how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: The lab's climate-nuclear-security project is foresight research on how climate change and an expansion of nuclear power bear on nuclear security and proliferation: further from the risk of nuclear war than arms-control work, so 0.4 (0.1 to 0.8), our judgment.

rows.label: Nuclear field work: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: The Nolan Center's nuclear work and the Converging Risks Lab's climate-nuclear project, each at its own multiplier, weighted by spending (right within one branch).
rows.formula: ((csw_line - fb_cost) * (1 - csw_bio_share) * csw_nuclear_evidence_adj + crl_line * crl_nuclear_share * crl_evidence_adj) / (nuclear_cost_share * program_spend)

rows.label: Policy win: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: Not used: the branch has no spending (pol_cost_share is 0). The template's range kept.

rows.label: Field-building: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: The alumni's work is valued at a typical dollar of the field's work (fb_work_dollars), so no further step for how far a typical project applies: 1 (0.7 to 1.2), the template's figure.

rows.label: AI field work: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Not used: the AI branch has no spending (weight 0). The template's figure kept.

rows.label: Pandemic field work: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Others work on biological weapons and biodefense policy (NTI | bio, the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, the Bipartisan Commission on Biodefense, RAND), but few convene allied governments on it: 0.7 (0.4 to 0.9), our judgment.

rows.label: Nuclear field work: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Many groups work on nuclear arms control (the Arms Control Association, NTI, the Federation of American Scientists, Carnegie), but each brings its own analysis: 0.7 (0.4 to 0.9), our judgment; that the work would have come years later is in years_of_impact.

rows.label: Policy win: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Not used: the branch has no spending (pol_cost_share is 0). The template's range kept.

rows.label: Field-building: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Who would have entered anyway is already out of fb_share_working: 1 (0.8 to 1), the template's figure.

rows.label: AI field work: this charity's share of the resources behind it

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): governments' budgets and enforcement, companies' compliance, the use others make of research. The charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work. Fixed.

rows.explainer: The dialogues and the tracker draw on outside experts' time beside CSR's staff; the allied officials who attend are the adopters, under the mobiliser's share, not in this one (docs/normalization.md 2.24). 0.9 (0.7 to 1), our judgment.

rows.label: Pandemic field work: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Nuclear field work: this charity's share of the resources behind it

rows.explainer: CSR's share among those who run the fellowships: 0.95 (0.7 to 1), the template's figure. The fellows' employers are mobilised, under the mobiliser's share (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Field-building: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Climate security: how far the chain's figures apply
rows.explainer: The chain's figures are already judgments of this work's effect, not a typical project's, but changes the past work won in US defence planning are being undone (the 2025 budgets' smaller size is in gov_public_dollars_per_dollar, not here): 0.7 (0.3 to 1.1), our judgment.

rows.label: Climate security: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Other groups work on climate and security (CNA's Military Advisory Board, the Wilson Center's Environmental Change and Security Program, the American Security Project, think tanks in allied countries); CSR's Center founded the field's main network of military leaders. 0.6 (0.3 to 0.9), our judgment, a crowded field.

rows.label: Climate security: CSR's share of the resources behind the change
rows.explainer: CSR's share among those who worked for the changes: the advisory board and the International Military Council's members give unpaid time beside CSR's staff and the Council's founding partners (IRIS, HCSS, Clingendael). The militaries' and agencies' own staff who carry out the changes, serving officers among them, are the adopters: their part is under the mobiliser's share, not in this one (docs/normalization.md 2.24). 0.8 (0.6 to 1), our judgment.

rows.label: Climate security: share of credit used

rows.label: How far the typical project's effect applies to this charity's work
rows.formula: (w_ai * ai_evidence_adj + w_bio * bio_evidence_adj + w_nuclear * nuclear_evidence_adj + w_pol * pol_evidence_adj + w_fb * fb_evidence_adj + w_gov * gov_evidence_adj) / (w_total)
rows.explainer: Applied: each branch's own multiplier (<branch>_evidence_adj), weighted by the branches' healthy years (w_<branch>), so that evidence_adj × counterfactual_adj × attribution_share is each branch's own product weighted by its value, never by its spending. The gov branch added beside the template's five.

rows.formula: (w_ai * ai_evidence_adj * ai_counterfactual_adj + w_bio * bio_evidence_adj * bio_counterfactual_adj + w_nuclear * nuclear_evidence_adj * nuclear_counterfactual_adj + w_pol * pol_evidence_adj * pol_counterfactual_adj + w_fb * fb_evidence_adj * fb_counterfactual_adj + w_gov * gov_evidence_adj * gov_counterfactual_adj) / (w_total * evidence_adj)
rows.explainer: Applied: each branch's own share (<branch>_counterfactual_adj), weighted by the branches' healthy years (w_<branch>) after evidence_adj, so that evidence_adj × counterfactual_adj × attribution_share is each branch's own product weighted by its value, never by its spending. The gov branch added beside the template's five.

rows.formula: (w_ai * ai_evidence_adj * ai_counterfactual_adj * ai_attribution_share + w_bio * bio_evidence_adj * bio_counterfactual_adj * bio_attribution_share + w_nuclear * nuclear_evidence_adj * nuclear_counterfactual_adj * nuclear_attribution_share + w_pol * pol_evidence_adj * pol_counterfactual_adj * pol_attribution_share + w_fb * fb_evidence_adj * fb_counterfactual_adj * fb_attribution_share + w_gov * gov_evidence_adj * gov_counterfactual_adj * gov_attribution_share) / (w_total * evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj)
rows.explainer: Applied: each branch's own share (<branch>_attribution_share), weighted by the branches' healthy years (w_<branch>) after the earlier factors, so that evidence_adj × counterfactual_adj × attribution_share is each branch's own product weighted by its value, never by its spending. The gov branch added beside the template's five.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Whether CSR's other funders (Coefficient Giving above all) would give less if small donors gave more is the room factor of @next_dollar.council_on_strategic_risks (docs/normalization.md 2.10), so it isn't asked again here (one question per adjustment): 1, our judgment; 0.85 to 1.05 for funging the room factor misses.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no outcome of CSR's work is measured, on the risks (a typical project's cut and forecast chances) or on public spending (the gov branch's chain is judged), so the shared missing-data step applies to every branch (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond what is counted, each part a share of the modelled value (about a quarter of it, after adjustments, the nuclear branch's): work against a single detonation or a limited nuclear war, which kills far fewer than 10% of people and has no shared forecast (nuclear_smaller_per_year 0), 1.4% (6% of the nuclear value); chemical weapons, which the Nolan Center covers in its framing but with no programme, 0.5%; the climate-security work's benefits beyond better public spending (militaries' disaster response, which its MiRCH tracker follows, conflict and displacement that planning may avert, militaries' own emissions), 0.5%: its counted value is under 0.1% of the total, so even a hundredfold more stays small. 2.5% (0 to 10%) in all, our judgment.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A typical project's chance of backfiring is already in the shared cut per dollar (Rethink Priorities' backfire step). CSR builds no capabilities: its biological work is policy and diplomacy against weapons programmes. 0, down to −3%, our judgment.

rows.label: Harm: information hazards and attention, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire: public analyses of biological threats and of where weapons are could point an adversary somewhere, and arguments about new nuclear systems feed debates either way; CSR's work is policy, not technical detail, and has not been shown to cause harm. 0, down to −5%, our judgment.
